You plan work the way an experienced lead would before staffing it: you pin down the real objective and every deliverable, work out the numbers, surface assumptions and risks, decide who is needed and what each person must know and produce, and build in checks. You plan for what the task actually requires, not for whatever tools happen to be installed.

# Task
A freight carrier in Indiana runs 20 Class 8 tractors on regional routes under 250 miles a day, about 60,000 miles per truck per year. Should it replace them with battery-electric tractors? Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel vs battery-electric: purchase price, any federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026, fuel/energy cost per mile (Indiana diesel price vs Indiana commercial electricity rate), charging infrastructure, and maintenance. Show the table, state every assumption, cite every figure with its date, and give a recommendation. Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.

Working interpretation (settled before planning; do not re-interpret it or guess otherwise):
- "Class 8 tractors" means US heavy-duty road tractors over 33,000 lb GVWR, sleeper or day cab unspecified
- "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" means Federal 45W commercial clean vehicle credit (up to $40,000 for over 14,000 lb), which may have expired for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025, plus any Indiana state or utility programs (an assumption)
- "Indiana diesel price" means EIA Midwest or Indiana average retail on-highway diesel price per gallon
- "Indiana commercial electricity rate" means EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh (an assumption)
- "charging infrastructure" means Depot DC fast chargers (about 150 kW) per truck or shared, with installation and utility upgrades
- "7-year total cost of ownership per truck" means Undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure over 7 years, net of incentives (an assumption)
The final answer must open with this line: I read "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" as Federal 45W commercial clean vehicle credit (up to $40,000 for over 14,000 lb), which may have expired for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025, plus any Indiana state or utility programs; if you meant Grant and rebate programs (EPA Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicles grants, VW settlement funds via IDEM, utility make-ready rebates) or Federal excise tax exemption and other tax treatment such as depreciation, the answer below may not apply. I read "Indiana commercial electricity rate" as EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh; if you meant A specific utility's commercial or EV tariff (Duke Energy Indiana, AES Indiana, NIPSCO, I&M) including demand charges, the answer below may not apply. I read "7-year total cost of ownership per truck" as Undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure over 7 years, net of incentives; if you meant Discounted TCO including residual or resale value at year 7, the answer below may not apply.

# Existing expert roles (reuse if they fit)
[]

# Tools the team will have when it runs (use them where they fit; do NOT let this list limit the plan)
- calc: evaluates an arithmetic expression such as 12 * (3 + 4) (installed)
- echo: returns its input unchanged (installed)
- web_search: searches the web and returns snippets with their URLs (a role that lists web_search or asks for it gets it)
- fetch_url: fetches the text of a web page (given together with web_search)
- local tools, sandboxed in the run's own workspace, no network: Bash (runs Python 3 or a shell command; python3 has openpyxl, python-docx, python-pptx, matplotlib, pypdf), Read, Write and Edit (files). A role gets them through a capability request for the ability (e.g. python_interpreter, file writing)
- local skills for document formats: xlsx, docx, pptx, pdf (a skill request for the format gives the role the skill's instructions and the local tools)
- a tool pool: plain code matches every capability request against cached MCP servers and skills; a request may be filled or may stay unfilled, so a step must say what to do without it

# History (your previous draft)


# Reviewer suggestions (latest round)


# How to plan
Work in this order and write each section.

1. Requirements. List every deliverable and requirement stated or clearly implied by the task, one per
   line with an id (R1, R2, ...). Keep the task's own verbs: "gather current", "prototype and test",
   "estimate", "deliver". Never weaken a requirement (e.g. "test" must stay "test", not "estimate").
2. Givens and derived numbers. List the numbers in the task and anything that follows from them
   (show the arithmetic). List assumptions you must make, each marked as an assumption.
   Open questions (optional): where the task is ambiguous and you settled it by an assumption, write
   each under "## Open Questions", one per line as "- question: ... | assumption: ...". Write None if
   nothing in the task was ambiguous. What the task's names and terms mean (which organisation, place, product
   or person it is about) is not yours to settle: when the task carries a "Working interpretation", plan on it
   exactly and do not guess another reading; if it is still unclear what the task is about, write the question
   with "assumption: not settled" rather than guessing.
3. Ideal capabilities. Before choosing roles, decide what abilities the work needs, as if any reasonable
   tool or skill were available. A TOOL is something that acts or fetches (web search, code execution,
   a database sandbox, a file reader). A SKILL is know-how or a method (cost modelling, schema design,
   GDPR transfer analysis, risk assessment). A document format (xlsx, docx, pptx, pdf) or a house style is a
   SKILL, not a tool.
4. Roles. Create the smallest team of well-defined specialists (at most 5 including the
   final writer) that covers every requirement. A role is well defined only if it has ALL of these fields:
   {
     "name": "Cloud Cost Analyst",
     "seniority": "senior",
     "description": "who they are and why they are on this team (2-3 sentences)",
     "goal": "the single outcome this role is accountable for",
     "responsibilities": ["...", "..."],
     "skills": ["managed-database pricing models", "TCO modelling", "..."],
     "tools": ["the tools this role ideally needs, installed or not"],
     "inputs": ["what it receives and from which step"],
     "outputs": [{"artifact": "cost table", "format": "markdown table: provider x db x monthly USD"}],
     "success_criteria": ["how we know the output is good enough"],
     "constraints": ["limits from the task, e.g. 12-person team, EU residency"],
     "covers": ["R2", "R3"],
     "is_summariser": false,
     "prompt": "the full working prompt for this specialist: persona, method step by step, what to check, and the exact output format. Write it as a senior practitioner would brief a peer."
   }
   Do not give a role a tool only to fill the field; an empty list is fine. Specialists produce the
   content (analysis, tables, plans); exactly one role has "is_summariser": true and only assembles and
   edits their outputs into the final deliverable — it creates no new analysis and has no tools.
5. Capability requests. For every tool or skill in step 3 that is not installed, add one request as a JSON
   blob with keys: name, kind (tool|skill), for_role, what_it_does, input, output, example_input,
   example_output. Requesting is expected and costs nothing now; hiding a need is a planning error.
6. Execution plan. Numbered steps. Each step's FIRST line must be "N. [Role A, Role B]: short title".
   Under it, indented lines:

           depends on (and is done by a role that did not produce them); everything else is work
     covers: R ids
     depends_on: step numbers (or none) — steps with no dependency between them may run in parallel
     do: what exactly happens, as sub-steps
     output: the artifact, starting with one or more format markers that plain code will check —
             table: (a markdown table), list: (a bulleted or numbered list), code: (a code block),
             memo: (a document with headings) — e.g. "output: table: provider x database x monthly USD"
     done_when: the check that ends the step
   Include at least one verification step where a different role checks numbers, sources or the
   prototype results before the final step. The final step is the summariser assembling the deliverable.
7. Risks and decision points. The main risks to the plan and where a decision must be made
   (for example "if residency rules out region X, re-run step 3").

A rough pre-calculation suggests BEV loses on a pure undiscounted 7-year basis without incentives, but sourced inputs must drive the answer, not my placeholders. The plan separates sourcing (incentives, market data) from modelling. An independent verifier then checks the numbers, sources and dates. The deliverable is a memo of at most 2 pages that opens with the mandated interpretation line. Page length is checked after rendering, not guessed.

R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel Class 8 tractors and for battery-electric Class 8 tractors (undiscounted, net of incentives, per the working interpretation).
R2: Determine purchase price for each powertrain (diesel and BEV Class 8 tractor), sourced and dated.
R3: Determine the federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026. This covers 45W status, Indiana state programs and utility programs. R4: Determine fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or EIA Midwest) on-highway diesel price vs Indiana EIA average commercial electricity rate, converted to $/mile using stated mpg and kWh/mile.
R5: Determine charging infrastructure cost for 20 trucks (about 150 kW depot DC chargers, installation, utility upgrades), expressed per truck.

R8: State every assumption.
R9: Cite every figure with its date.
R10: Give a recommendation (replace, pilot, or defer), including whether the 250-mile/day duty cycle is feasible for BEV.
R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.

- given: 20 Class 8 tractors; Indiana; regional routes under 250 mi/day; about 60,000 mi/truck/yr; 7-year horizon.

- assumption: diesel at about 6.5 mpg and BEV at about 1.7–2.0 kWh/mi (to be sourced from manufacturer/NREL/CALSTART data).

- assumption: depot charging on-site, one 150 kW DC port per truck, with a shared-charger sensitivity.
- assumption: constant real prices (no escalation) in the base case. Diesel ±25% and electricity ±25% are sensitivities.

## Risks and Decisions:
- 45W status: if the primary source shows it ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, the base case has $0 federal credit. A hypothetical 45W case appears only as a labelled sensitivity. If the source shows otherwise, re-run steps 3–8.
- 30C charger credit: it likely ends mid-2026 and is limited to eligible census tracts. Count it only if confirmed for the depot's location; otherwise $0.
- BEV purchase price is volatile and often negotiated. Decision at step 3: use the base case plus low/high, and let the recommendation rely on the breakeven rather than a single point.
- Range feasibility: if the feasibility note finds most BEV tractors cannot reliably do 250 mi/day, the recommendation becomes "pilot on shorter routes or defer", and the TCO assumes a fleet of the longer-range (and costlier) models.
- Demand charges and the actual tariff could make the effective electricity rate much higher than the EIA average. This is disclosed and shown in the sensitivity; it is outside the base case by the working interpretation.
- Missing sourced values (e.g. no public price for a BEV model): label them as estimates with their basis, and let the verifier mark them Unverified. Do not hide them.
- The 2-page limit may force trimming. Cut prose before numbers or dates. If over length at step 8, move secondary sensitivities out and keep the table, incentives, assumptions and sources.
- Excluding residual value and discounting favours neither option clearly, but it could understate the BEV if resale is strong. The memo says so in one line.

R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel Class 8 tractors and for battery-electric Class 8 tractors (undiscounted, net of incentives, per the working interpretation).

R4: Determine fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or EIA Midwest) on-highway diesel price vs Indiana EIA average commercial electricity rate, converted to $/mile using stated mpg and kWh/mile.

R6: Determine maintenance cost per mile for diesel vs BEV, sourced and dated.
R7: Show the TCO table (diesel vs BEV, by cost component, per truck over 7 years).
R8: State every assumption.
R9: Cite every figure with its date.
R10: Give a recommendation (replace, pilot, or defer), including whether the 250-mile/day duty cycle is feasible for BEV.
R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.
R12: Open the memo with the mandated interpretation line, verbatim.

## Givens and Assumptions
- given: 20 Class 8 tractors; Indiana; regional routes under 250 mi/day; about 60,000 mi/truck/yr; 7-year horizon.
- derived: lifetime miles per truck = 60,000 × 7 = 420,000 mi. Fleet miles per year = 20 × 60,000 = 1,200,000 mi.
- derived: average daily miles = 60,000 / ~250 operating days = 240 mi/day, so the "under 250" cap is binding on most days.
- derived (illustrative placeholders, to be replaced by sourced values):
  - Diesel at 6.5 mpg → 60,000 / 6.5 ≈ 9,231 gal/yr. At $3.80/gal that is ≈ $35,100/yr, or $0.585/mi.
  - BEV at 2.0 kWh/mi → 120,000 kWh/yr at the vehicle. With 90% charger efficiency, 120,000 / 0.9 ≈ 133,300 kWh from the grid. At $0.12/kWh that is ≈ $16,000/yr, or $0.267/mi.
  - Energy saving ≈ $19,100/yr × 7 ≈ $134k per truck.
  - Maintenance: diesel $0.20/mi vs BEV about $0.14/mi → 0.06 × 420,000 ≈ $25k saving.

- assumption: purchase price inputs are new 2026 model-year list/typical street prices, not fleet-negotiated.
- assumption: diesel at about 6.5 mpg and BEV at about 1.7–2.0 kWh/mi (to be sourced from manufacturer/NREL/CALSTART data).
- assumption: no residual value, no discounting, and no financing cost, per the working interpretation. Residual and NPV appear only as a one-line caveat.
- assumption: the EIA average commercial rate excludes demand charges; the memo flags this as the largest tariff risk and runs a sensitivity.
- assumption: federal excise tax (12%) on heavy truck retail sales applies to both powertrains unless a source shows otherwise. It is included in purchase price if the sourced prices exclude it.
- assumption: depot charging on-site, one 150 kW DC port per truck, with a shared-charger sensitivity.
- assumption: constant real prices (no escalation) in the base case. Diesel ±25% and electricity ±25% are sensitivities.

- derived: average daily miles = 60,000 / ~250 operating days = 240 mi/day, so the "under 250" cap is binding on most days.

- assumption: constant real prices (no escalation) in the base case. Diesel ±25% and electricity ±25% are sensitivities.

## Risks and Decisions:
- 45W status: if the primary source shows it ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, the base case has $0 federal credit. A hypothetical 45W case appears only as a labelled sensitivity. If the source shows otherwise, re-run steps 3–8.
- 30C charger credit: it likely ends mid-2026 and is limited to eligible census tracts. Count it only if confirmed for the depot's location; otherwise $0.
- BEV purchase price is volatile and often negotiated. Decision at step 3: use the base case plus low/high, and let the recommendation rely on the breakeven rather than a single point.
- Range feasibility: if the feasibility note finds most BEV tractors cannot reliably do 250 mi/day, the recommendation becomes "pilot on shorter routes or defer", and the TCO assumes a fleet of the longer-range (and costlier) models.
- Demand charges and the actual tariff could make the effective electricity rate much higher than the EIA average. This is disclosed and shown in the sensitivity; it is outside the base case by the working interpretation.
- Missing sourced values (e.g. no public price for a BEV model): label them as estimates with their basis, and let the verifier mark them Unverified. Do not hide them.
- The 2-page limit may force trimming. Cut prose before numbers or dates. If over length at step 8, move secondary sensitivities out and keep the table, incentives, assumptions and sources.
- Excluding residual value and discounting favours neither option clearly, but it could understate the BEV if resale is strong. The memo says so in one line.

The decision depends on four things. First, whether the BEV purchase premium and the 20-truck charger cost exceed the energy and maintenance savings over 420,000 miles. Second, whether any incentive survives in 2026; 45W appears to have ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, but this must come from primary sources. Third, whether a 250-mile day is feasible on one overnight charge. Fourth, how sensitive the result is to the Indiana diesel price and the real tariff, including demand charges. Research is split into incentives and market data, run in parallel and independent of the model. An independent reviewer checks the model, then the memo draft. The quality gate says the summariser may own only the last step, so the TCO Modeller, who owns the numbers, drafts the memo text, including fleet-level figures. The writer only builds the .docx, renders it, and confirms length and the opening line.

## Requirements:
R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel and for battery-electric Class 8 tractors.
R2: Gather current purchase prices for a comparable diesel Class 8 tractor and for BEV tractors, sourced and dated.
R3: Determine which federal and Indiana incentives actually apply to a purchase in 2026 (45W, 30C, excise tax, Indiana state, utility, grant programs). Mark each applies / does not apply / unclear, with date and source.
R4: Gather fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or EIA Midwest) on-highway diesel price vs the Indiana EIA average commercial electricity rate, converted with stated mpg and kWh/mi.
R5: Estimate charging infrastructure cost for 20 trucks (about 150 kW depot DC chargers, installation, utility upgrades), per truck and for the fleet.
R6: Gather maintenance cost per mile for diesel and BEV, sourced and dated.
R7: Show the TCO table (diesel vs BEV, by cost component, per truck over 7 years).
R8: State every assumption.
R9: Cite every figure with its date.
R10: Give a recommendation (replace, pilot or defer), including whether the 250 mi/day duty cycle is feasible for BEV.
R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.
R12: Open the memo with the mandated interpretation line, verbatim.
R13: The carrier runs 20 Class 8 tractors on regional routes under 250 mi/day. Model that fleet, giving per-truck and ×20 fleet figures (TCO difference, charging total) computed by the modeller, not the writer.
R14: Plan the decision: list what the carrier must supply (depot location, serving utility and tariff, operating days) and the next steps.
R15: Read "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" as the working interpretation (45W plus Indiana state and utility programs) and apply it.
R16: Read "Indiana commercial electricity rate" as the EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in c/kWh and apply it. Demand charges appear only as a labelled sensitivity.

# Task
A freight carrier in Indiana runs 20 Class 8 tractors on regional routes under 250 miles a day, about 60,000 miles per truck per year. Should it replace them with battery-electric tractors? Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel vs battery-electric: purchase price, any federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026, fuel/energy cost per mile (Indiana diesel price vs Indiana commercial electricity rate), charging infrastructure, and maintenance. Show the table, state every assumption, cite every figure with its date, and give a recommendation. Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.

Working interpretation (settled before planning; do not re-interpret it or guess otherwise):
- "Class 8 tractors" means US heavy-duty road tractors over 33,000 lb GVWR, sleeper or day cab unspecified
- "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" means Federal 45W commercial clean vehicle credit (up to $40,000 for over 14,000 lb), which may have expired for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025, plus any Indiana state or utility programs (an assumption)
- "Indiana diesel price" means EIA Midwest or Indiana average retail on-highway diesel price per gallon
- "Indiana commercial electricity rate" means EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh (an assumption)

- "7-year total cost of ownership per truck" means Undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure over 7 years, net of incentives (an assumption)

I read "Indiana commercial electricity rate" as EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh; if you meant A specific utility's commercial or EV tariff (Duke Energy Indiana, AES Indiana, NIPSCO, I&M) including demand charges, the answer below may not apply. ## Thought
The decision turns on four things: how much the BEV purchase premium and charger cost exceed the energy and maintenance savings over 420,000 miles; whether any incentive survives in 2026 (45W appears to have ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, so it must be confirmed from primary sources); whether a 250-mile day is operationally feasible on a battery; and how sensitive the result is to the Indiana diesel price and electricity tariff. A rough pre-calculation suggests BEV loses on a pure undiscounted 7-year basis without incentives, but sourced inputs must drive the answer, not my placeholders. The plan separates sourcing (incentives, market data) from modelling. An independent verifier then checks the numbers, sources and dates. The deliverable is a memo of at most 2 pages that opens with the mandated interpretation line. Page length is checked after rendering, not guessed.

## Requirements:
R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel Class 8 tractors and for battery-electric Class 8 tractors (undiscounted, net of incentives, per the working interpretation).
R2: Determine purchase price for each powertrain (diesel and BEV Class 8 tractor), sourced and dated.
R3: Determine the federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026. This covers 45W status, Indiana state programs and utility programs. R4: Determine fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or EIA Midwest) on-highway diesel price vs Indiana EIA average commercial electricity rate, converted to $/mile using stated mpg and kWh/mile.

R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.

- given: 20 Class 8 tractors; Indiana; regional routes under 250 mi/day; about 60,000 mi/truck/yr; 7-year horizon.

- derived: average daily miles = 60,000 / ~250 operating days = 240 mi/day, so the "under 250" cap is binding on most days.
- derived (illustrative placeholders, to be replaced by sourced values):

- assumption: purchase price inputs are new 2026 model-year list/typical street prices, not fleet-negotiated.
- assumption: diesel at about 6.5 mpg and BEV at about 1.7–2.0 kWh/mi (to be sourced from manufacturer/NREL/CALSTART data).
- assumption: no residual value, no discounting, and no financing cost, per the working interpretation. Residual and NPV appear only as a one-line caveat.
- assumption: the EIA average commercial rate excludes demand charges; the memo flags this as the largest tariff risk and runs a sensitivity.
- assumption: federal excise tax (12%) on heavy truck retail sales applies to both powertrains unless a source shows otherwise. It is included in purchase price if the sourced prices exclude it.
- assumption: depot charging on-site, one 150 kW DC port per truck, with a shared-charger sensitivity.
- assumption: constant real prices (no escalation) in the base case. Diesel ±25% and electricity ±25% are sensitivities.

## Risks and Decisions:
- 45W status: if the primary source shows it ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, the base case has $0 federal credit. A hypothetical 45W case appears only as a labelled sensitivity. If the source shows otherwise, re-run steps 3–8.
- 30C charger credit: it likely ends mid-2026 and is limited to eligible census tracts. Count it only if confirmed for the depot's location; otherwise $0.
- BEV purchase price is volatile and often negotiated. Decision at step 3: use the base case plus low/high, and let the recommendation rely on the breakeven rather than a single point.
- Range feasibility: if the feasibility note finds most BEV tractors cannot reliably do 250 mi/day, the recommendation becomes "pilot on shorter routes or defer", and the TCO assumes a fleet of the longer-range (and costlier) models.
- Demand charges and the actual tariff could make the effective electricity rate much higher than the EIA average. This is disclosed and shown in the sensitivity; it is outside the base case by the working interpretation.
- Missing sourced values (e.g. no public price for a BEV model): label them as estimates with their basis, and let the verifier mark them Unverified. Do not hide them.
- The 2-page limit may force trimming. Cut prose before numbers or dates. If over length at step 8, move secondary sensitivities out and keep the table, incentives, assumptions and sources.
- Excluding residual value and discounting favours neither option clearly, but it could understate the BEV if resale is strong. The memo says so in one line.

You plan work the way an experienced lead would before staffing it: you pin down the real objective and every deliverable, work out the numbers, surface assumptions and risks, decide who is needed and what each person must know and produce, and build in checks. You plan for what the task actually requires, not for whatever tools happen to be installed.

# Task
A freight carrier in Indiana runs 20 Class 8 tractors on regional routes under 250 miles a day, about 60,000 miles per truck per year. Should it replace them with battery-electric tractors? Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel vs battery-electric: purchase price, any federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026, fuel/energy cost per mile (Indiana diesel price vs Indiana commercial electricity rate), charging infrastructure, and maintenance. Show the table, state every assumption, cite every figure with its date, and give a recommendation. Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.

Working interpretation (settled before planning; do not re-interpret it or guess otherwise):
- "Class 8 tractors" means US heavy-duty road tractors over 33,000 lb GVWR, sleeper or day cab unspecified
- "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" means Federal 45W commercial clean vehicle credit (up to $40,000 for over 14,000 lb), which may have expired for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025, plus any Indiana state or utility programs (an assumption)
- "Indiana diesel price" means EIA Midwest or Indiana average retail on-highway diesel price per gallon
- "Indiana commercial electricity rate" means EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh (an assumption)
- "charging infrastructure" means Depot DC fast chargers (about 150 kW) per truck or shared, with installation and utility upgrades
- "7-year total cost of ownership per truck" means Undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure over 7 years, net of incentives (an assumption)
The final answer must open with this line: I read "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" as Federal 45W commercial clean vehicle credit (up to $40,000 for over 14,000 lb), which may have expired for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025, plus any Indiana state or utility programs; if you meant Grant and rebate programs (EPA Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicles grants, VW settlement funds via IDEM, utility make-ready rebates) or Federal excise tax exemption and other tax treatment such as depreciation, the answer below may not apply. I read "Indiana commercial electricity rate" as EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in cents/kWh; if you meant A specific utility's commercial or EV tariff (Duke Energy Indiana, AES Indiana, NIPSCO, I&M) including demand charges, the answer below may not apply. I read "7-year total cost of ownership per truck" as Undiscounted sum of purchase, energy, maintenance and infrastructure over 7 years, net of incentives; if you meant Discounted TCO including residual or resale value at year 7, the answer below may not apply.

# Existing expert roles (reuse if they fit)
[]

# Tools the team will have when it runs (use them where they fit; do NOT let this list limit the plan)
- calc: evaluates an arithmetic expression such as 12 * (3 + 4) (installed)
- echo: returns its input unchanged (installed)
- web_search: searches the web and returns snippets with their URLs (a role that lists web_search or asks for it gets it)

## Thought
The decision turns on four things: how much the BEV purchase premium and charger cost exceed the energy and maintenance savings over 420,000 miles; whether any incentive survives in 2026 (45W appears to have ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, so it must be confirmed from primary sources); whether a 250-mile day is operationally feasible on a battery; and how sensitive the result is to the Indiana diesel price and electricity tariff. A rough pre-calculation suggests BEV loses on a pure undiscounted 7-year basis without incentives, but sourced inputs must drive the answer, not my placeholders. The plan separates sourcing (incentives, market data) from modelling. An independent verifier then checks the numbers, sources and dates. The deliverable is a memo of at most 2 pages that opens with the mandated interpretation line. Page length is checked after rendering, not guessed.

## Requirements:
R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel Class 8 tractors and for battery-electric Class 8 tractors (undiscounted, net of incentives, per the working interpretation).
R2: Determine purchase price for each powertrain (diesel and BEV Class 8 tractor), sourced and dated.
R3: Determine the federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026. This covers 45W status, Indiana state programs and utility programs. It also covers other federal items that change the price (excise tax, 30C charger credit). Each must be stated as applicable or not, with the date and source.
R4: Determine fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or EIA Midwest) on-highway diesel price vs Indiana EIA average commercial electricity rate, converted to $/mile using stated mpg and kWh/mile.
R5: Determine charging infrastructure cost for 20 trucks (about 150 kW depot DC chargers, installation, utility upgrades), expressed per truck.
R6: Determine maintenance cost per mile for diesel vs BEV, sourced and dated.
R7: Show the TCO table (diesel vs BEV, by cost component, per truck over 7 years).
R8: State every assumption.
R9: Cite every figure with its date.
R10: Give a recommendation (replace, pilot, or defer), including whether the 250-mile/day duty cycle is feasible for BEV.
R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.
R12: Open the memo with the mandated interpretation line, verbatim.

## Givens and Assumptions:
- given: 20 Class 8 tractors; Indiana; regional routes under 250 mi/day; about 60,000 mi/truck/yr; 7-year horizon.
- derived: lifetime miles per truck = 60,000 × 7 = 420,000 mi. Fleet miles per year = 20 × 60,000 = 1,200,000 mi.
- derived: average daily miles = 60,000 / ~250 operating days = 240 mi/day, so the "under 250" cap is binding on most days.
- derived (illustrative placeholders, to be replaced by sourced values):
  - Diesel at 6.5 mpg → 60,000 / 6.5 ≈ 9,231 gal/yr. At $3.80/gal that is ≈ $35,100/yr, or $0.585/mi.
  - BEV at 2.0 kWh/mi → 120,000 kWh/yr at the vehicle. With 90% charger efficiency, 120,000 / 0.9 ≈ 133,300 kWh from the grid. At $0.12/kWh that is ≈ $16,000/yr, or $0.267/mi.
  - Energy saving ≈ $19,100/yr × 7 ≈ $134k per truck.
  - Maintenance: diesel $0.20/mi vs BEV about $0.14/mi → 0.06 × 420,000 ≈ $25k saving.
  - Charging load: 250 mi × 2.0 = 500 kWh/day. At 150 kW and 90% efficiency that is about 3.7 h per truck, so one charger per truck overnight is plausible. Shared chargers need a schedule check.
- assumption: purchase price inputs are new 2026 model-year list/typical street prices, not fleet-negotiated.
- assumption: diesel at about 6.5 mpg and BEV at about 1.7–2.0 kWh/mi (to be sourced from manufacturer/NREL/CALSTART data).
- assumption: no residual value, no discounting, and no financing cost, per the working interpretation. Residual and NPV appear only as a one-line caveat.
- assumption: the EIA average commercial rate excludes demand charges; the memo flags this as the largest tariff risk and runs a sensitivity.
- assumption: federal excise tax (12%) on heavy truck retail sales applies to both powertrains unless a source shows otherwise. It is included in purchase price if the sourced prices exclude it.
- assumption: depot charging on-site, one 150 kW DC port per truck, with a shared-charger sensitivity.
- assumption: constant real prices (no escalation) in the base case. Diesel ±25% and electricity ±25% are sensitivities.

## Open Questions:

- question: Are residual value and discounting wanted? | assumption: no; undiscounted, per working interpretation.

## Risks and Decisions:
- 45W status: if the primary source shows it ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, the base case has $0 federal credit. A hypothetical 45W case appears only as a labelled sensitivity. If the source shows otherwise, re-run steps 3–8.
- 30C charger credit: it likely ends mid-2026 and is limited to eligible census tracts. Count it only if confirmed for the depot's location; otherwise $0.
- BEV purchase price is volatile and often negotiated. Decision at step 3: use the base case plus low/high, and let the recommendation rely on the breakeven rather than a single point.
- Range feasibility: if the feasibility note finds most BEV tractors cannot reliably do 250 mi/day, the recommendation becomes "pilot on shorter routes or defer", and the TCO assumes a fleet of the longer-range (and costlier) models.
- Demand charges and the actual tariff could make the effective electricity rate much higher than the EIA average. This is disclosed and shown in the sensitivity; it is outside the base case by the working interpretation.
- Missing sourced values (e.g. no public price for a BEV model): label them as estimates with their basis, and let the verifier mark them Unverified. Do not hide them.
- The 2-page limit may force trimming. Cut prose before numbers or dates. If over length at step 8, move secondary sensitivities out and keep the table, incentives, assumptions and sources.
- Excluding residual value and discounting favours neither option clearly, but it could understate the BEV if resale is strong. The memo says so in one line.

## Thought
The decision turns on four things:
- **Cost gap:** whether the BEV purchase premium plus the 20-truck charger cost exceeds the energy and maintenance savings over 420,000 miles.
- **Incentives:** whether any incentive survives in 2026. 45W appears to have ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, but this must be confirmed from primary sources.
- **Duty cycle:** whether a 250-mile day is feasible on one overnight charge.
- **Sensitivity:** how far the result moves with the Indiana diesel price and the real tariff, including demand charges.

Incentive research and market-data research run in parallel and independently of the model. A different role reviews the model, and later the memo draft. The Modeller owns every number and drafts the memo text, including fleet ×20 figures. The summariser owns only the last step: it builds the .docx, renders it to count pages, and reads the opening line and table back from the saved file.

## Requirements
R1: Compute a 7-year total cost of ownership per truck for diesel and for battery-electric Class 8 tractors.
R2: Gather current purchase prices for a comparable diesel Class 8 tractor and for BEV tractors, sourced and dated.
R3: Determine which federal and Indiana incentives actually apply to a purchase in 2026 (45W, 30C, excise tax, Indiana state, utility, grant programs). Mark each applies / does not apply / unclear / depends on location, with date and source.
R4: Gather fuel/energy cost per mile: Indiana (or EIA Midwest) on-highway diesel price vs the Indiana EIA average commercial electricity rate, converted with stated mpg and kWh/mi.
R5: Estimate charging infrastructure cost for 20 trucks (about 150 kW depot DC chargers, installation, utility upgrades), per truck and for the fleet.
R6: Gather maintenance cost per mile for diesel and BEV, sourced and dated.
R7: Show the TCO table (diesel vs BEV, by cost component, per truck over 7 years).
R8: State every assumption.
R9: Cite every figure with its date.
R10: Give a recommendation (replace, pilot or defer), including whether the 250 mi/day duty cycle is feasible for BEV.
R11: Deliver a Word (.docx) memo of at most 2 pages.
R12: Open the memo with the mandated interpretation line, verbatim.
R13: Run the numbers for the carrier's 20 Class 8 tractors on regional routes under 250 mi/day, giving per-truck and ×20 fleet figures (TCO difference, charging total) computed by the modeller, not the writer.
R14: Plan the decision: list what the carrier must supply (depot location, serving utility and tariff, operating days) and the next steps.
R15: Read "federal and Indiana incentives that actually apply to a purchase in 2026" as the working interpretation (45W plus Indiana state and utility programs) and apply it.
R16: Read "Indiana commercial electricity rate" as the EIA average commercial retail price for Indiana in c/kWh and apply it. Demand charges appear only as a labelled sensitivity.

  - Fleet figure = per-truck difference × 20.

- assumption: no residual value, no discounting, no financing cost (working interpretation).
- assumption: the EIA statewide commercial average excludes demand charges. A demand-charge-inflated rate is a labelled sensitivity, sourced to a utility tariff sheet if found, otherwise labelled an assumption with its basis.
- assumption: depot charging on site, one 150 kW DC port per truck, with a shared-charger sensitivity if the feasibility note allows it.
- assumption: constant real prices. Diesel ±25% and electricity ±25% are sensitivities.
- assumption: 250 operating days per year (labelled; the carrier must confirm).
- assumption: depot location and serving utility are unknown. 30C and utility make-ready therefore count as $0 in the base case unless confirmed, and the memo lists them as items the carrier must confirm.
